epilogue

EP-ih-log -- three syllables, stress on the first syllable, EP. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Epilogue is a concluding section at the end of a book or play.

Don't skip the epilogue -- it reveals who finally ended up keeping the dog.

Example

The mystery wraps up on page 300: culprit caught, jewels returned. Then comes the epilogue, set a full year later -- the inspector, retired now and tending her garden, opens her mailbox to find a postcard with no signature, only a drawing of a jewel. She smiles.

An epilogue is a concluding section that comes after the main story has already ended, giving readers one last glimpse -- what became of everyone, and sometimes one final tease. Epilogues often announce themselves with a time jump: 'ten years later...'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

afterword: An afterword is the author stepping outside the story to speak in their own voice -- how the book came to be, whom to thank. An epilogue stays inside the story: the characters are still on stage, living one last scene after the main ending.

finale: A finale is the last, biggest moment of a performance -- the closing number, the fireworks -- built for applause. An epilogue is quieter and comes after the real ending: one more glimpse of the characters once the main story is already over.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

prologue: an opening section before the story begins

preface: an author's introductory note

Where it sits · how artful the final piece is

conclusion → epilogue → coda

conclusion vs. epilogue: Conclusion sits below epilogue in craft: every essay and story has a conclusion, simply because everything ends, while an epilogue is a deliberate extra scene, returning to the characters after the ending has already done its work.

coda vs. epilogue: Coda is the strongest and most artful: borrowed from music, it names a deliberately crafted tailpiece added after the ending proper -- exactly the flourish a well-written epilogue provides.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — epi-: upon, in addition (Greek)

root — logue: word, speech (Greek logos)

Put it together: Epilogue is Greek for 'words added on' -- epi- ('upon, in addition') plus logos ('word, speech'). In ancient theater, the epilogos was the speech delivered after the play was over, when an actor stepped forward to add a few final words. The word still means exactly that: the extra words laid on top of a finished story.

Use the root in a new word: prologue: The director cut the prologue entirely from the final version of the film.

Root Check

Word Choice

Epilogue and prologue are bookends: the prologue speaks before the story, the epilogue after it. An epilogue usually continues the story itself -- often after a time jump -- showing what became of the characters; an afterword, by contrast, is typically the author stepping out of the story to speak as themselves. If the characters are still on stage, it is an epilogue.
